SEATTLE, Washington (CNN) -- Predicting the path of a swine flu outbreak is next to impossible, public health officials say. But Dr. Ira Longini has spent more than three decades trying to do just that. Dr. Ira Longini studies simulations of hypothetical influenzas and how they would spread. And Longini says the apparent new strain of swine flu appears to be here to stay. "We are probably going to have to live with this virus for some time," he told CNN. Longini specializes in the mathematical and statistical theory of epidemics. He works at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Institute at the Hutchinson Research Center in Seattle, Washington. The researcher studies simulations of hypothetical influenzas and how they would spread across the United States. For the moment, he said, there is not enough information about the swine flu that has sickened hundreds in Mexico and about 50 people in the United States to accurately forecast how the disease will travel. But Longini's simulations of a fictional killer flu that were ordered by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) show the importance of steps health officials can take to prevent further spread of the virus. These measures include "social distancing," or encouraging those sickened with the flu to stay home or seek medical treatment; closing places where groups of people gather; and making anti-flu medications available to large portions of the population. In the simulations, Longini said, these forms of containment reduce the sickness by nearly two-thirds. "The name of the game is to slow transmission until a well-matched vaccine can be made and distributed. I am fairly optimistic we can do that," he said.  Watch how computer models simulate an outbreak's spread » . So far, Longini said, it appears that everyone sickened by swine flu in the United States contracted the disease while traveling in Mexico, the apparent epicenter of the outbreak. But he cautioned: "That could change very fast. Obviously people in these communities could also get on airplanes and go other places or get on buses or cars or trucks and move around. The picture may change very rapidly. Basically, influenza is going to go where people go." Health officials agree that the worst may still be yet to come. "It is too soon for us to say what the spectrum is," Dr. Richard Besser, the acting director of the CDC, said Monday on Larry King Live. "We are going to see cases in this country that are more severe, individuals who are hospitalized, and I would not be surprised if we see deaths in this country." Longini said health officials are doing everything they can to mitigate how widely the swine flu spreads in the United States. Even if authorities examined everyone entering the country, Longini said, it would not solve the problem. "Through simulations and mathematical work we've shown that travel restrictions -- although potentially useful in slowing spread [of swine flu] -- they are not going to stop it," Longini said. "We can screen airline passengers, but there all those asymptomatic or incubating people we would miss. So you really have to deal with these outbreaks locally, everywhere they are occurring."  Watch how countries are scanning travelers » . Longini said he hopes that as more data come in about the outbreak, it will help to answer questions researchers have about why the swine flu appears more deadly in the Mexico cases than the ones in the United States. Researchers also hope to find out why such a large percentage of fatalities in Mexico are young people whose healthy immune systems usually protect them from the flu. But there is good news, Longini said, at least temporarily, for populations in certain areas. In North America and Europe, summer will soon begin, ending the traditional flu season. Even outbreaks such as swine flu tend to follow standard flu season patterns, he said. Other parts of the world may not be so lucky. "Timing is terrible for people in the Southern Hemisphere -- places like New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, parts of South America, "Longini said. "They are just coming into their flu season."

Longini studies simulations of hypothetical influenza viruses and how they might spread. He says the apparent new strain of swine flu appears to be here to stay.

“We are probably going to have to live with this virus for some time,” he told CNN.

Longini specializes in the mathematical and statistical theory of epidemics. He works at the Vaccine and Infectious Disease Institute at the Hutchinson Research Center in Seattle, Washington, where he studies simulations of hypothetical influenza viruses and how they would spread across the United States.

For now, he said, there is not enough information about the swine flu that has sickened hundreds of people in Mexico and about 50 in the United States to accurately forecast how the disease will spread.

However, Longini’s simulations of a fictional killer flu, commissioned by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), demonstrate the importance of measures health officials can take to prevent the virus from spreading further.

These measures include “social distancing,” or encouraging people sickened by the flu to remain at home or seek medical treatment; closing places where groups of people gather; and making anti-flu medications available to large portions of the population.

In the simulations, Longini said, these forms of containment reduced illness by nearly two-thirds.

“The name of the game is to slow transmission until a well-matched vaccine can be made and distributed. I am fairly optimistic we can do that,” he said.

*Watch how computer models simulate the spread of an outbreak »*

So far, Longini said, it appears that everyone sickened by swine flu in the United States contracted the disease while traveling in Mexico, the apparent epicenter of the outbreak.

But he cautioned: “That could change very fast. Obviously, people in these communities could also get on airplanes and go other places, or get on buses or cars or trucks and move around. The picture may change very rapidly. Basically, influenza is going to go where people go.”

Health officials agree that the worst may still be to come.

“It is too soon for us to say what the spectrum is,” Dr. Richard Besser, acting director of the CDC, said Monday on *Larry King Live*. “We are going to see cases in this country that are more severe, individuals who are hospitalized, and I would not be surprised if we see deaths in this country.”

Longini said health officials are doing everything they can to mitigate the spread of swine flu in the United States. Even if authorities examined everyone entering the country, he said, it would not solve the problem.

“Through simulations and mathematical work, we’ve shown that travel restrictions—although potentially useful in slowing the spread [of swine flu]—are not going to stop it,” Longini said. “We can screen airline passengers, but there are all those asymptomatic or incubating people we would miss. So you really have to deal with these outbreaks locally, everywhere they are occurring.”

*Watch how countries are screening travelers »*

Longini said he hopes that, as more data about the outbreak become available, they will help answer researchers’ questions about why swine flu appears to be more deadly in Mexico than in the United States.

Researchers also hope to determine why such a large percentage of the fatalities in Mexico involve young people, whose healthy immune systems usually protect them from the flu.

But there is good news, Longini said—at least temporarily—for populations in certain regions. Summer will soon begin in North America and Europe, bringing the traditional flu season to an end. Even outbreaks such as swine flu tend to follow standard seasonal flu patterns, he said.

Other parts of the world may not be so fortunate.

“Timing is terrible for people in the Southern Hemisphere—places like New Zealand, Australia, South Africa, parts of South America,” Longini said. “They are just coming into their flu season.”

Epidemiologist Ira Longini studies infectious diseases by creating mathematical models of the ways people interact at home, at work, at school, and in the wider community. Using computer simulations, he can introduce a new influenza strain—such as the H1N1 virus commonly called swine flu—into a virtual population and observe how quickly it might spread. Researchers can then change assumptions about the virus or the public-health response to compare possible outcomes.

Such models are especially valuable at the beginning of a pandemic, when a vaccine designed for the new strain may not yet be available. Producing and distributing a well-matched vaccine can take months, so health officials need measures that can slow transmission in the meantime. Longini’s simulations examined strategies including social distancing, closing schools and other gathering places, isolating infected people, and distributing antiviral medicines on a large scale.

The results suggested that no single intervention would be enough. Used together, however, these measures could have a substantial effect. Reducing close contact makes it harder for the virus to pass from one person to another, while antiviral drugs can shorten illness and decrease infectiousness when given promptly. In the simulated outbreaks, a coordinated response reduced the total number of infections by nearly two-thirds.

Computer models cannot predict an epidemic with complete certainty. Their conclusions depend on assumptions about the virus, human behavior, drug availability, and how quickly authorities act. Nevertheless, they allow researchers and policymakers to test strategies without waiting for a real-world crisis. They can also identify logistical problems, such as how many antiviral courses would be needed or which communities should receive assistance first.

The main benefit of containment may be time rather than the complete elimination of the disease. Slowing an outbreak can ease pressure on hospitals, reduce illness and deaths, and give scientists additional weeks or months to manufacture and distribute an effective vaccine. Longini’s work therefore shows how mathematical modeling can help public-health officials prepare for influenza pandemics and choose combinations of measures that offer the greatest protection.

# Computer models map swine flu’s path — and ways to slow it

**ATLANTA, 2009** — As the newly identified H1N1 “swine flu” virus spread across borders, epidemiologist Dr. Ira Longini turned to computer simulations to answer two urgent questions: How quickly could the outbreak grow, and what could public health officials do to contain it?

Longini’s models simulated thousands of people moving through households, schools, workplaces and communities. By estimating how often infected people passed the virus to others, the programs could project the epidemic’s likely course and test potential interventions before they were deployed.

The simulations suggested that the 2009 H1N1 virus could spread rapidly because most people had little immunity to the new strain. Children and young adults appeared especially important in transmission, making schools a central focus of containment planning.

But the models also indicated that no single measure was likely to stop the outbreak once sustained community transmission had begun.

The most effective strategy, according to Longini’s modeling work, would combine several steps: quickly identifying cases, treating infected patients with antiviral drugs, providing preventive medication to close contacts when feasible, isolating sick people and reducing opportunities for person-to-person transmission. Temporary school closures and other social-distancing measures could slow the spread, particularly early in an outbreak.

Speed was critical. Antiviral containment worked best when officials recognized cases quickly and intervened before infections became widespread. Delays, shortages of medication or a virus that proved more contagious than expected could sharply reduce the chances of containing it.

Vaccination offered the strongest long-term protection, the models suggested, but developing and distributing a vaccine would take months. That meant communities might have to rely initially on antivirals, voluntary isolation, hygiene measures and temporary changes to school or workplace operations.

Longini’s research also underscored the limits of travel restrictions. Because influenza can spread before many patients seek medical care — and because some infections cause only mild symptoms — screening travelers or closing borders was unlikely to keep the virus out indefinitely. Such measures might delay its arrival, but they would not necessarily prevent community transmission.

Public health experts cautioned that computer models are not crystal balls. Their projections depend on assumptions about the virus’s contagiousness, the length of the infectious period, existing immunity and how people respond to official guidance. In the early stages of the 2009 outbreak, many of those factors remained uncertain.

Still, the models gave officials a way to compare strategies and prepare for different scenarios. Their central message was clear: Early action could buy valuable time, layered interventions could reduce illness, and vaccination would ultimately be crucial — but once a novel influenza virus was spreading widely, complete containment would be difficult.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how mathematical simulations can forecast a swine flu outbreak, including social distancing, antiviral drugs, travel restrictions, vaccination, and seasonal differences between hemispheres.
counterfactuals.output:
Mathematical simulations forecast a swine flu outbreak by representing how infections move through a population and then testing how interventions alter that movement.

### 1. Basic epidemic model

A common model divides people into groups such as:

- **Susceptible**: able to become infected  
- **Exposed**: infected but not yet infectious  
- **Infectious**: able to transmit the virus  
- **Recovered or removed**: immune, isolated, or deceased  
- **Vaccinated or treated**: protected to varying degrees  

An SEIR model uses equations such as:

\[
\frac{dS}{dt}=-\beta(t)\frac{SI}{N}, \qquad
\frac{dE}{dt}=\beta(t)\frac{SI}{N}-\sigma E
\]

with additional equations for infectious and recovered people. Here, \(\beta(t)\) represents transmission, while \(\sigma\) and the recovery rate describe incubation and infectious periods.

More detailed **agent-based models** simulate individuals, households, schools, workplaces, hospitals, and travel networks. Models are calibrated with surveillance data, laboratory-confirmed cases, hospitalizations, deaths, contact surveys, and mobility information.

### 2. Social distancing

School closures, remote work, gathering limits, masks, and voluntary contact reduction are modeled by lowering the number or infectiousness of contacts. This reduces the effective reproduction number:

\[
R_t \approx R_0 \times \text{remaining contact fraction} \times \text{susceptible fraction}
\]

Simulations estimate whether distancing can:

- Delay the epidemic peak  
- Reduce peak hospital demand  
- Lower total infections  
- Prevent \(R_t\) from remaining above 1  

Models should also account for people shifting contacts—for example, children may meet outside school—so closing schools does not necessarily eliminate all transmission.

### 3. Antiviral drugs

Antivirals can be represented as:

- Shortening the infectious period  
- Reducing infectiousness when treatment starts early  
- Lowering the chance of severe illness or death  
- Preventing infection in exposed household contacts  

The forecast depends on stockpile size, distribution speed, treatment timing, adherence, and possible drug resistance. Simulations can compare treating only severe cases with rapid treatment of all symptomatic cases or prophylaxis of close contacts.

### 4. Travel restrictions

Cities or countries are connected in a **metapopulation network**, with infections carried between locations by air, road, rail, and sea travel. Restrictions are modeled by reducing passenger flows or screening and isolating travelers.

These measures often delay introduction into new locations rather than prevent it entirely, because:

- Infected people may travel before symptoms appear  
- Restrictions are rarely complete  
- Local transmission may already be established  

Nevertheless, even a short delay can provide time to distribute antivirals, prepare hospitals, or begin vaccination.

### 5. Vaccination

Vaccination moves some susceptible people into a partially or fully protected group. Models include:

- Vaccine effectiveness against infection and severe disease  
- Time needed to manufacture and distribute doses  
- Delay of roughly one or more weeks before immunity develops  
- Number of doses required  
- Uptake by age and risk group  
- Reduced protection if the vaccine is poorly matched to the strain  

Simulations compare strategies such as prioritizing children, healthcare workers, high-contact groups, pregnant people, or those at greatest risk of hospitalization. Vaccinating high-contact groups may reduce transmission most efficiently, while vaccinating high-risk groups may prevent more severe outcomes.

### 6. Seasonal differences between hemispheres

Influenza transmission varies seasonally because of temperature, humidity, indoor crowding, school calendars, and possibly changes in immunity. Models often make transmission seasonal:

\[
\beta(t)=\beta_0\left[1+a\cos\left(\frac{2\pi(t-\phi)}{365}\right)\right]
\]

The phase \(\phi\) is shifted by about six months between the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Consequently, a new strain introduced during one hemisphere’s winter may spread rapidly there while growing more slowly in the other hemisphere’s summer. The second hemisphere may then experience a later wave when its winter begins. Tropical regions may have weaker or rainfall-associated seasonality and can help sustain transmission between temperate-season peaks.

### 7. Forecasting scenarios and uncertainty

The model is run thousands of times under different assumptions about infectiousness, immunity, behavior, intervention timing, and seasonality. It produces ranges—not exact predictions—for:

- Timing and size of epidemic peaks  
- Total infections and symptomatic cases  
- Hospital and intensive-care demand  
- Deaths  
- Geographic spread  
- Effects of individual and combined interventions  

The most useful forecasts are updated repeatedly as new data arrive. They typically show that layered measures—early distancing, rapid antiviral use, targeted travel measures, and timely vaccination—perform better than any single intervention, but the result depends heavily on how quickly and consistently each measure is implemented.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**BREAKING: U.S. braces for wider spread of H1N1 as cases emerge beyond Mexico**

*Public-health officials say travel screening may identify some sick passengers but cannot contain a virus that can spread before symptoms appear.*

**WASHINGTON, April 27, 2009** — A newly identified strain of H1N1 influenza is likely to spread further from Mexico into the United States, public-health experts warned Monday, as governments intensified surveillance and urged hospitals to watch for patients with flu-like symptoms.

Cases have already been confirmed in several U.S. states, suggesting the virus has crossed borders and may be spreading within communities. Officials cautioned that the number of infections could rise quickly as testing expands.

“We don’t think we can contain the spread of this virus,” Dr. Anne Schuchat, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s interim deputy director for science and public-health programs, told reporters. The focus, she said, must shift toward reducing illness, detecting severe cases and protecting people at greatest risk.

The outbreak was first linked to a surge of respiratory illness in Mexico, but international travel and the ordinary movement of people between Mexico and the United States make additional cases inevitable, influenza specialists said. Flu viruses spread primarily through respiratory droplets and close contact, allowing infected travelers to transmit the virus before health authorities know they are sick.

Airport screening — including temperature checks and questionnaires — may detect some visibly ill passengers, but experts say it cannot reliably stop influenza. People can be infected without yet having a fever, may suppress symptoms with medication or may become sick only after completing their journey. Screening also does little to address spread across land borders or within local communities.

Dr. Keiji Fukuda, the World Health Organization’s acting assistant director-general for health security and environment, said the virus’s geographic reach made containment unrealistic. “Containment is not a feasible option,” he told reporters, emphasizing the need for surveillance, treatment and measures to limit the outbreak’s effects.

Authorities advised travelers and the broader public to wash their hands frequently, cover coughs and stay home when ill. People with severe breathing problems or other serious symptoms were urged to seek medical care.

Officials stressed that the outbreak’s eventual severity remained uncertain. Although severe illness and deaths had been reported in Mexico, many confirmed U.S. cases were comparatively mild. Researchers were working to determine how readily the virus spreads, which groups face the greatest danger and whether existing antiviral medicines remain effective.

Public-health agencies were expected to report additional cases as laboratories processed a growing backlog of samples.

# CDC turns to computer models and local containment as swine flu spreads

### Federal health officials warn it is too early to predict a U.S. death toll, while the Southern Hemisphere faces the added danger of the virus arriving as winter begins

**ATLANTA — May 2009** — As cases of a new strain of swine-origin influenza multiply across the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is using computer models, laboratory surveillance and reports from local health departments to answer a question with no easy solution: How severe could the outbreak become?

The models are not crystal balls. They calculate possible outcomes using assumptions about how quickly the H1N1 virus spreads, how many infections become serious, whether schools and workplaces accelerate transmission, and how effectively antivirals and other public-health measures are deployed.

At this early stage, many of those variables remain uncertain.

That means federal officials can outline a range of scenarios but cannot responsibly provide a firm estimate of how many Americans may die. A virus that spreads efficiently but usually causes mild illness would produce a very different toll from one that sends a larger share of patients to hospitals or returns in a more severe wave later in the year.

## Modeling the outbreak

CDC epidemiologists are feeding confirmed and probable cases, hospitalizations, deaths, age patterns and geographic spread into models designed to estimate the virus’s transmissibility and likely trajectory.

Among the most important measurements is the virus’s reproduction rate: the average number of people infected by each sick person in a population with little immunity. Even a modest change in that number can produce dramatically different results over several generations of transmission.

Officials are also studying:

- The time between one infection and the next;
- The proportion of infections that never reach a doctor;
- Hospitalization and fatality rates by age group;
- The effectiveness and timing of antiviral treatment;
- The impact of school closures and reduced public gatherings;
- Existing immunity among older adults;
- The possibility of a second wave during the regular fall flu season.

Early case counts are particularly difficult to interpret. Testing initially focuses on people sick enough to seek medical care, which can make the virus appear more dangerous than it is. At the same time, delays in testing and reporting can make the outbreak appear smaller.

As broader surveillance identifies mild and previously undetected cases, estimates of severity may change—sometimes substantially.

## From national guidance to local containment

With cases appearing in multiple states, the CDC’s strategy is shifting away from the idea that every infection can be stopped at the border or contained through intensive tracing.

Instead, the agency is emphasizing “community mitigation”: slowing transmission enough to protect vulnerable people and prevent hospitals from being overwhelmed.

Local health departments are central to that effort. Depending on the severity of an outbreak, their tools may include:

- Asking sick people to remain at home;
- Separating symptomatic patients in clinics and emergency rooms;
- Tracing and monitoring close contacts in limited settings;
- Providing antivirals to patients at high risk of complications;
- Closing schools when illness or absenteeism makes normal operations difficult;
- Restricting visits at hospitals and long-term-care facilities;
- Canceling or modifying large public events;
- Expanding laboratory testing and hospital surveillance.

The CDC has revised some recommendations as evidence accumulates. Early in the outbreak, officials took a more aggressive approach to school closures around confirmed cases. As it became clear that infections were already spreading in communities—and that many illnesses were relatively mild—the agency moved toward more targeted decisions based on local conditions, absenteeism and disease severity.

That change illustrates a central challenge of outbreak management: measures that make sense when only a few cases exist may become disruptive and less useful once community transmission is established.

Prolonged school closures, for example, can reduce contact among children but also force parents to miss work, disrupt meals and other services, and create staffing problems for hospitals and emergency agencies. Children may also continue to gather elsewhere, reducing the benefit.

## How many Americans could die?

No credible early estimate can be reduced to a single number.

Pandemic-planning models have historically examined scenarios ranging from an outbreak resembling seasonal influenza to a catastrophe approaching the 1918 pandemic. Those planning figures are designed to test hospital capacity and supply needs; they are not forecasts for the new H1N1 virus.

The potential death toll depends on both the virus’s fatality rate and the number of people infected. A relatively low fatality rate can still lead to a substantial number of deaths if tens of millions become ill. Conversely, alarming early fatality figures may fall as health authorities discover a larger number of mild cases.

Officials are watching closely for severe disease among pregnant women, young children, people with asthma or other chronic conditions, and those with weakened immune systems. One unusual feature of the outbreak is that many infections are occurring among children and younger adults, rather than being concentrated among the elderly as seasonal influenza often is.

Older adults may have some partial immunity from exposure to distantly related influenza viruses, but researchers have not yet determined how protective that immunity might be.

For comparison, seasonal influenza already causes thousands to tens of thousands of U.S. deaths in a typical year, depending on the circulating strains and the method used to estimate mortality. A pandemic virus could add to that burden, especially if it returns during the fall and winter.

The CDC is therefore preparing for more than the outbreak visible now. Officials are considering hospital demand, antiviral stockpiles, protective equipment, testing capacity and the possible development of an H1N1-specific vaccine.

## The Southern Hemisphere’s winter warning

The most immediate international concern may be south of the equator, where the new virus is arriving as countries enter their regular influenza season.

Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Argentina, Chile and other Southern Hemisphere nations could face simultaneous circulation of the new H1N1 strain and seasonal flu viruses. That overlap could complicate diagnosis, increase pressure on hospitals and create opportunities for influenza viruses to exchange genetic material.

Scientists emphasize that genetic reassortment does not automatically produce a more dangerous virus. Still, the possibility is one reason laboratories are sequencing viral samples and monitoring for changes in transmissibility, severity and antiviral resistance.

The Southern Hemisphere may also provide an early indication of how H1N1 behaves in winter conditions. Influenza generally spreads more efficiently during colder months, when people spend more time indoors and lower humidity may help viral transmission.

If the virus causes a large winter wave there, Northern Hemisphere governments could gain valuable—but troubling—information before their own fall season. They may learn which age groups are most vulnerable, how quickly hospitals fill, whether antivirals remain effective and whether school-based transmission drives broader community spread.

Countries with limited medical resources face the greatest risk. Intensive-care beds, ventilators, laboratory tests and antivirals are unevenly distributed, and a surge that wealthy nations might manage could strain or overwhelm poorer health systems.

## Buying time

For now, the CDC’s objective is less about eliminating the virus than buying time.

Slowing transmission can spread cases over a longer period, giving hospitals a better chance to cope and scientists more time to evaluate vaccine options. It can also help health officials refine their models as better data arrive.

The public-health message remains straightforward: people with fever and respiratory symptoms should stay home except to seek medical care, cover coughs and sneezes, wash their hands frequently and contact a medical professional if they develop warning signs such as difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion or severe dehydration.

Behind those simple recommendations is a far more complicated calculation—one being revised daily as new laboratory results and local reports reach Atlanta.

The ultimate U.S. toll will not be determined by computer models alone. It will depend on the biology of the virus, the speed of public-health action, the resilience of local hospitals and how communities respond if the first wave is only the beginning.

*Historical note: The virus became known as the 2009 H1N1 pandemic strain. The CDC later estimated that from April 2009 through April 2010 it caused approximately 60.8 million U.S. cases, 274,000 hospitalizations and 12,469 deaths, with substantial uncertainty around each estimate.*
